projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with James Workman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran James R. Workman. Mr. Workman served with the U.S. Army 25th Infantry division, 35th Regiment, Third Battalion. He served in the Pacific theater and Mr. Workman is a veteran of Pearl Harbor. His highest rank was staff sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and we recorded this at Mr. Workman's home in Willoughby, Ohio on January 10th, 2002, and that was Jim's 81st birthday.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941? Were you already in the Army?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No, sir. I enlisted September 7th, 1939.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: When they bombed us, I only had six days to go when they bombed us. I was ready to come home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your unit? What --

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I was in the 25th Division, 35th Infantry, Company M.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I was staff sergeant. I was in the motor pool.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I run -- charge of the trucks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you got over to Hawaii, 1939?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was it like back then?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: It was a beautiful island. It was beautiful. It was an island then. Now it's -- you've been there and it's all commercialized. Now it's all skyscrapers. Not like it used to be. But army life was no good. There's -- we only made 21 dollars a month when I enlisted as a private. And had no money. There was no women there. So many servicemen. The whole fleet was there. The Army we had 20-some thousand soldiers there and they had the Marines. It was just nothing but servicemen. You go down to Honolulu and you seen nothing but servicemen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So a vast majority of the population was servicemen back then?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yep. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it was pretty good to be stationed there for a couple years?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: It was beautiful. The island, the weather's perfect. You couldn't beat the weather. You had a beautiful island and everything. You know, you are a young kid. You're homesick. You wanted to get home. End up being gone for six years. Never made it home for -- until the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you didn't get any leaves at all?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: If you would have, where would you go? I mean them days, they didn't have the jets. They had them propeller jobs, but you had to have this to go. And 21 dollars a month.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Ain't gonna do no flying, that's for sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It certainly would take too long to try to take a boat to the mainland, right?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Well, it's -- I don't know how many days it would take. Us, we're in no hurry. That ship was a transport that done about 11 knots, so you're barely moving, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was your job there? Were you basically training the whole time you were there?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah. In fact, before the war started -- two weeks before the war started, we were out on intensive jungle warfare training. It was the first time they had issued us gas masks and live ammunition. First time. And steel helmets. We was out for two weeks. We come in on a Saturday, went down to Honolulu and raised a little dickens and come back up, and next morning it happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. All right. Well, I guess --

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: It shattered me because I'm counting every hour. I had six days to go, wanting to come home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So where exactly were you stationed?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: At the Scofield barracks. Scofield Barracks at the Army base, Scofield barracks. We was about a mile and a half from Wheeler Field. That's what they really wanted, Wheeler Field. They bombed us a little bit. They strafed us, but they didn't do much damage to the Army barracks. Mostly it was Wheeler Field, but the main blunt, the Navy got. They wanted the Navy and they got it. Them was the boys that really got it. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. Let's go back there then. Saturday night, what were you doing, December 6th?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Honolulu.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Having fun?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Drinking beer and having fun, yep. Never dreaming and counting the hours to come home naturally. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. All right. The morning of December 7th, did you sleep in?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Well, no. We got up. We had our breakfast and lounging around. They had porches called lanai in Hawaii. It's all screened in. Some of the guys out there reading papers and looking out and this and that. The planes starting coming over. They used a few curse words, so and so, P-40s with their wheels down. I bet you we're going back out on maneuvers. Because there was rumors about a war. I mean everything pointed to a war between us and Japan. Everything pointed to it. But we figured we was going back out on maneuvers. It was P-40s with their wheels down, unless we started seeing the big rising suns and we knew.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your first thought and the thoughts of those around you when you realized?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Everybody was so scared and so excited and running in circles. Our guns were in the armory on -- we had gun racks down in the armory. We called it armory down in the supply room. They were locked up. We had to bust the locks to get to our guns and anything that flew over, we shot at it. Anything that flew over. We had reports there was invasion that night. They'd said there was paratroopers were landing and just everybody was, you know -- also we had orders if -- any lights, shoot it out. That's the way it was. But everybody was so excited and mixed up. Nobody knowed what was going on. It seemed nobody knowed what was going on. And there was nothing going on that night. Just the guys shooting at anything. Like I said, anybody had a light on -- they had orders: If there was a light, you shoot it out. Another guy shot cows. Anything that moved. Scared.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were you actually in the barracks or eating breakfast when it happened?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Just had -- finished breakfast. We were in the barracks and we all run out on the quadrangle -- that's the square between the barracks -- ran out on quadrangle and we finally got our rifles and there was planes going everywhere. Everywhere you looked there was airplanes. We were shooting at them. Couldn't hit them, but we were shooting at them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Shooting at them with rifles?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Rifles, yep. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Some of the officers had .45s. Anything to shoot at them. Like sling shots, you couldn't hit nothing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you said there was some strafing of that area?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah, they did -- they strafed. They dropped bombs in our area. They strafed. Not many bombs but probably the pilots were excited as we were and they just dropped a few of them. But main thing they wanted the Navy and Air Force, which they did. They got that, yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you realize the scope of -- could you see Pearl Harbor from where you were?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: You could see the smoke. You could see the smoke. The island burned for two days. You could see the black smoke all over the island, yeah, you could see that. And Wheeler Field was just a mile away, just blazing black smoke.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long did it take you to realize the scope of what was going on?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Not too long. It didn't take very long. But, like I say, everybody was running around, didn't know what to do and excited. We just -- we couldn't believe it, but yet everything looked like it was coming.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other stories or memories that you have from that day?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: That night, that afternoon we'd been down to Ft. Shafter and you could see the bodies laying on the lawn. Hundreds of bodies laying out in the open. Just we brought them in and put them on the lawn. That's all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No. None. Not there. Not that day, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Nope.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was the mood on the island in the next couple of days?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: They started stringing barbed wire everywhere they could. They started cutting trees down, so in case they landed, you'd have a field of fire for your machine guns and rifles and so on and a lot of activity. Guns being moved everywhere, artillery pieces and so on, just preparing for the invasion which we thought was coming and it didn't. If it would have, they would have taken Hawaii, too. They had nothing to stop them. Old war equipment, World War I, we couldn't have stopped them. Just like the Philippines, they would have taken Hawaii and they probably would have thrown in the West Coast, too. They had nothing to stop them. No Navy. Nothing. They had the Air Force, most of the planes. There's nothing to stop them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long did the rumors persist that they were coming?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Well, for weeks. Weeks after the attack. It was preparing it for the invasion. There's rumors that we knew they were going to come and blah, blah, blah and so on, but thank God they didn't at that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long did you stay there then in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Till the following November. Then we sailed for Guadalcanal, South Pacific. Three Army divisions. We relieved the Marines on Guadalcanal. We were 27 days in the Alaman Sea Cor(ph). After 27 days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any memories at Guadalcanal then?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Mosquitoes. I got rheumatic fever. They evacuated me to New Caledonia. They evacuated me to the Fijis. I come back, and they evacuated me to Auckland, New Zealand. I come back. They evacuated me to Brisbane, Australia. I come back. They took me back to Auckland, New Zealand, and from there recurring attacks of malaria fever and then they sent me to the States to Letterman General in Frisco. From there they sent me to Ft. McCloskey Hospital in Temple, Texas. That's close to Waco, Texas. I come home the first time in six years. Secured for a 30-day convalescent furlough and they give me my discharge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were dealing with this fever for a few years then?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the fever again?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Malaria.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Malaria? It was malaria?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: They called it recurrent attacks. I just kept getting malaria fever. You'd be weak and dysentery and shaking. You know in the tropics. You'd faint and you'd drop. They kept evacuating me. They finally got the message and discharged me -- I mean send me -- finally got back to the States.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they kept thinking that you were better sending you back --

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, yeah, sure. They needed every man. You know, every man counts in a war. They didn't care.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you did not really spend a lot of time on line because you were mostly in the hospital?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I spent was on -- board ship, like I was telling my friends and my wife. I put up for four months on the ocean and I was a soldier. In other words, you didn't fly in them days. You got on a troop transport or a naval cargo ship.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Jim, how about they reported you missing?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: All my personal stuff was on the ship and it was sunk. I lost all my personal stuff. I wasn't on the ship. My personal stuff was on the ship. And it --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: No. I'm talking about missing in action.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They had me missing in action, too. My parent -- my mother got the message that I was missing in action. That's 'cause they was sending me from one hospital to another. And my one sister -- she's still living. She just turned 83 this January 1st -- she traced me down in Letterman General Hospital, San Francisco. She finally found out where I was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But they basically lost track of you?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Missing in action. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they sent an official telegram to your family saying you were missing in action?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did they ever apologize?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You mentioned you lost some buddies then at Guadalcanal?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: On Guadalcanal, different islands, Talogi, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any specific memories of those guys?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Just the one, our company clerk. He was shot. Sniper got him, and my battalion commander, Lt. Col. Reese, he got shot right between the eyes. Sniper got him. And I was his bodyguard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Even when the war started, he told me you stick with me. We're side by side. We sleep together. Your rifle's right beside us. We were buddy buddies and he got shot.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's go back to a little earlier in '42. Do you remember the Doolittle raid?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction to that?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: We were thrilled to death. We were thrilled to death. And I -- like I -- my wife don't like for me to tell this. When we was in Hawaii for our 50th anniversary, I had my Pearl Harbor survivor's cap on. My wife and I was waiting for a bus in Honolulu. There was an old Jap sitting in a bus station, a little portable bus station. He says, "I see you veteran you. You was here in '41?" I says, "Yeah." "50 years, what do you think of the Japanese now?" "We had only two bombs. We should have dropped a hundred on you." I looked him right in the eyes. I meant what I said. We should have wiped them off the face of the map. Something you don't realize what they were. They were inhuman. You know about the Bataan death march what they did and so on. You're helpless. You're a soldier. You're a prisoner. You got dysentery. You get weak. You got malaria. You drop to your knees. They stick a bayonet in you. That's human. I still feel we should have wiped them off the face of the map. Because today they own us. We buy all their junk.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did he react to that at all when you said that?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: He just looked at me. He hung his head. My wife don't like it. She don't like it one bit. That's just exactly the way I feel. I'll never change. As long as I live to be 181, I'll tell him -- look him in the eye and tell him, "We should have wiped you off the map."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's certainly understandable.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. Any other specific memories of Guadalcanal?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No, just the mosquitoes and the Japs. That's all. One incident, we had a cargo landing craft beached. They come in and beach them, unload them. The ramp was down. The Japs come over. It was in May. I think May of '42 -- '42, I think. They strafed it and sent out tracers and set it on fire and 13 of the guys was roasted. Roasted. Blowed it up. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's see. The day FDR died, do you remember that day?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: The day what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The day Roosevelt died?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yes. Distinctly. I was telling my neighbor -- I was already home discharged. I was telling my neighbor. Her name is Evelyn Jennings. I said, "Evelyn, did you hear Roosevelt died?" She said, "What's the joke?" I says, "No joke. He died." She says, "Come on. What's the joke?" I said, "Turn your radio on." That was before we had TV. I said, "Turn your radio on." Yep. That's before your time. To me, he was the greatest president we ever had. It was -- nobody had anything when he got in. There was no jobs. There was nothing. He started the WPA, CC camps. He put people back to work. He was a great man for the working man.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you believe any of the rumors that Roosevelt knew Pearl Harbor was going to happen?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No. We -- it's not a rumor. We were almost positive he knew. We were almost positive. Anything. We servicemen. Everything pointed to it. Even civilians should have known because he goaded -- he goaded them. Eventually we was going to get into it anyhow, but he give England in 50 -- First World War, 50 of them, he put soldiers up in Iceland, Greenland. He had orders shoot on sight German submarines. And the Japanese, well, he cut off all our scrap and all our oil and stuff in the embargo. He just kept agitating, agitating and finally we got into it. I think he knew. I think all the messages, everything, I don't think anybody could make mistakes we made at that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Of course Pearl Harbor was a logical target?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Most logical target in the Pacific?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: There's an Army -- there's an Army -- I forget his name, Army man, an officer. He predicted that years and years before it happened. He says, second time, Pearl Harbor. He said it would be perfect. Perfect. The Japs knew how the Americans are, down in Honolulu celebrating the feast time, hey, love everybody, don't worry about nothing. They come in early Sunday morning, five minutes till 8:00. They had it planned right down to a T.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They knew the patterns of Americans as far as Sunday morning?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: The Japs, the population of Hawaii, civilians was about 70 percent Japanese. They had spies everywhere. They watched every ship coming in and out of that harbor. They watched the planes as they come and went. They had everything pinpointed. Even sugar cane fields. I don't know if this is true or not, but we heard rumors they had big arrows, sugar cane fields plowed, big arrows pointed at different targets. That was rumors we had. I don't know if it was true or not.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nobody discovered that for certain, though?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Our tailor, he was a Japanese lieutenant commander in the Japanese Navy. Our tailor, that tailored our uniforms. Japanese lieutenant commander.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was the feeling toward the Japanese after the attack on the island?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: We hated them all. If you had slant eyes, you needed shot. That was our feeling.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But there were too many to herd together and put in a camp, right?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: They said -- they said when the war started, 70 percent of the population was Japanese. 70 percent. Not many Hawaiians. Japanese.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did they catch any of the spies?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. They caught quite a few of them. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there any reaction among the Hawaiians that were not Japanese towards those that were Japanese?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I don't know. I'd be lying. I don't know. I don't know. The Japanese are a beautiful race of people. They're so friendly. They love everybody. They're a beautiful race and when the war started, boy, did they lean over backwards to us. Bringing us hot coffee out in the field. If we had to go anywhere, they'd take us if they had any kind of a vehicle. They lay out their home to you. The same way with the New Zealanders. I never met such friendly people in my life. They were so friendly towards the Americans.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So were you back home probably when VE Day happened, right?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about that day?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I went to town in my uniform and I knew all the girls was kissing me, I know that. Don't tell my wife that. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And then when you heard the news they dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that day?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: That was a big day, beautiful day. Yeah. Yep. It worked. Yep. How soon we gonna get some more? You know, wipe them off the map. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It seemed very obvious that the Japanese weren't going to give in before that?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Nope. No. Nope. Huh-uh. They're fanatics. They would like to die for their country. We tried to oblige them. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did -- was there any rumors or any idea of the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No. No. Nothing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That just came out of nowhere?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Nothing. Nothing. That was a big -- a well-kept secret. I never heard -- I never heard anybody, not anything. Not even a hint, a secret weapon or any kind of a super bomb, never. Never. Huh-uh. Huh-uh. Never.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So VJ Day, what were you doing on VJ Day?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Drinking beer and celebrating.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Was it as big a celebration as VE Day?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: To me, it was a lot bigger. Yep. They were both great days, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: -- but being involved in the South Pacific, VJ was the big one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after the war?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No. Huh-uh. Huh-uh. Never. Never give it a problem. In fact, for about -- until the last couple years, I didn't even talk about it. I mean I didn't -- just blot it out of my mind, you know, until I got involved with this Pearl Harbor buddy of mine. He's from back in my hometown. He's our president, Frank Luschka. He's been talking to me, this and that. We're different ones. We're way up in the years. We've been talking about it, different people been asking us different stuff, this and that. But before that, I blotted it out of my mind. Just forgot all about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other particularly vivid memories come to mind about Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No. We went down -- my battalion commander, Lt. Col. Reese, he was very interested. We went down and watched them repair the Nevada. They had repaired it to battleship and battleships -- he'd want to go down to Pearl Harbor and look around and he said let's go down, buddy, and see what they're doing. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You weren't involved in any salvage efforts?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No, not the Army. The Army was in some, but I don't know nothing about.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did you do down to Battleship Row and see the Arizona and the whole thing?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: You mean during the war?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: After the attack.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes. Yeah. Uh-huh. Everything was just tore up. Just junk laying everywhere. Scrap. You could see torches, torches, flashes everywhere, repairing what they do and so on. Cut up what they could cut up to get rid of and so on. And the big -- some of the battleships, we heard that they took some of the big 16-inch guns and put them up on Diamond Head. Coastal guns. Coast artillery. We heard they did that, but that was secret, too, you know. You didn't get involved in that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. How soon after the attack was it that you were able to get down there and look at that?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: About two weeks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: About two weeks?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: About two weeks, yeah. Things started calming down and getting back -- not to normal, but getting back to where you could think a little bit straight and so on, so forth. Like I said, this battalion commander, Lt. Col. Reese, he wanted to know what was going on down there. We'd get in the command car and drive him down.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your feelings when you first looked at that, what was happening? What had happened?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: How soon we gonna pay 'em back, double? Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, at that point two weeks later, if I remember correctly, there was still guys in the Oklahoma, right?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Got them out?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: It was laying right on its side. It was a pitiful sight.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else come to mind? Nothing jumps out, huh?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No. No. You blot a lot of it out, you know. Yeah. Never happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Never happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you've talked to more Pearl Harbor survivors recently in the --

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- last couple years?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: We have our chapter. We meet once a month down in the flats. Usually there's 12 to 15 of us in the whole greater Cleveland area left. We meet once a month. My wife goes with me and we go down there and have a cold beer and do a little lying. You know, beer's 50 cents a can. You can't beat it. You can't beat it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: They have a Frigidaire. They have beer if anybody wants. They have a couple fifths there if you want a shot. Talk to your buddies a while. Poor guys are in a wheelchair, trying to get around. Hey, honey, do you have that paper handy, that picture?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Your picture?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: After I seen you December 7th, that evening, they -- I didn't know this. Show --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Did you see this?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes, I did see that. I saw it after, too. Yeah. Yeah. That's great. So you had a busy day that day?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: I was on all three channels. They had me on TV. They had me on -- my niece was coming home from college. She said she and her girlfriend were driving. She says, "Oh, my God, that's my -- my granddad." They had me on the radio, you know. And different ones phoned, "We seen you on Channel 3. We seen you on Channel 5. We seen you on Channel 8." And Leon Bibbs, I went to community college -- Leon Bibbs talked to me and interviewed me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think I saw that. Channel 3 probably, right?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Channel 3, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I saw this the next day and realized I had you on my list.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: How many of them people phoned me and they seen me. They said we seen you in the paper. I said, "My God. You got to be kidding." When I got up the next morning, I got my paper out. Holy mackerel. You got to be kidding.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They knew you were --

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I'm looking. I'm looking -- people says how come you're looking so grim there. I've done this three years in a row now. First our president says, "Jim, carry the flag." Because I'm bragging I'm active. Like I said, most of the guys, they can't even walk up that submarine. He says, "No. No. You take the wreath." I says, "Okay." I says, "When do I" -- this is my third year. I never know when to throw the wreath in the water. I knew after taps, when after Taps. They says, "Jim, there's a big colored guy about six-foot-six." He says, "Man, I'll give you the signal." I said, "Okay." So all the people's down on the wharf, you know. Right then I'm looking, I'm trying to look to find him. I can't find him. Somebody behind me says something. I turned around and looked at them. I threw it in the water. I should have skipped it. Article in the second page there was -- they said I -- right here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: They said I should have skipped it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, when you went back there, there are still some bullet holes in the turrets?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yes. In Hickam Field, the one -- the one hangar, it's just pock-marked with cannon shell and bullet, 50-caliber bullet holes -- not holes, but indented in the cement.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you see the movie?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: We had a special invitation, a preview before it came out. We went to Pearl Harbor veterans and our wives. We went to view it. Got the little dog tag, too, don't you, that they gave us?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Somewhere.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: They gave us a little dog tag. It was fairly authentic, but it was so damned loud, they had those mikes all around and just booming and booming. I said come on already.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: But the movie was good.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Even the guy out was taking tickets from people and when I went to the rest room, he said, "What do you think of the movie?" I said, "It stinks." He said, "What?" I said, "It stinks. It's so damned loud." He said, "That's the way they wanted it." I said, "They can have it."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It did seem to take them a long time to get to Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And they apparently --

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: And it -- excuse me. You know what was so fake about that movie.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: We got our rank. We made corporals and sergeant. We made more money. But 90 percent of the guys were buck privates. We made 21 dollars a month in them days. Now they're making around seven or eight hundred dollars a month. We made 21 dollars a month. It showed those guys in this movie down in Honolulu drinking all the time. Where the hell did they get the money?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They're good for it.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I told one of the guys that. I want to ask you a question. I says, "You see something funny about this movie?" He says, "What?" Where in the hell did them birds get the money? They're drinking whiskey and stuff and they got all them girlfriends." I bet the guy who made that movie never give that a thought.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm sure that's true.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: You know, another thing, in 9- -- in 95 percent of the girls down there that the guys had them were officers, they had the money. Because they had check jobs. They weren't -- they had check jobs. How could a guy making 21 dollars a month pay for room and board for a broad, you know? It's just common logical sense. But the officers, they made the money and they had the girls.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you do -- you mentioned playing guitar, playing a little music. What other kinds of things did you do for entertainment?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: We had all kinds of sports. We went to our football games and basketball and baseball games. Any kind of sports there was, plus all of our training and so forth. You had your duties, you know. When you was off duty, we went to the post theater. It cost 20 cents to go to the show. We used to get a book that cost two dollars, show ticket, we call them show gadgets. We used to play poker, get a stack of them. You go to the movies. When the war started, we started getting -- I used to say the soldiers got all the popular brands of cigarettes. Well, I smoked. I smoked three packs a day. We used to get 75 cigarettes in a Planter's Peanut can standing on their ends, 75 of them. Chelsea, Piedmonts or Coppertones. There was no Lucky Strikes, no Camels. Huh-uh. Chelsea, Piedmonts, Coppertones. That was cigarettes we'd get.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So let's get back to music. Did you make up any songs?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: No. We just played the banjo. We used to play hillbilly. I had four brothers. We all played music. Me and my four brothers, when I came back from the war, we'd go to my mother's house Saturday night early. We'd play music and then we'd go out to the bar and --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Did you tell them you met your brother down there?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yeah. My brother was stationed at Ft. Kamehameha in Hawaii. So when I joined the Army, September 7, 1939, there was no openings in the States. You couldn't get in the Army in the United States. We had a small army. They had Panama, Hawaii or Philippines. I took Hawaii because my brother was down in Fort Kamehameha, 15th Coast Guard Artillery. That's right down at -- right at Pearl Harbor, entrance to Pearl Harbor. He went there three months before I went down, so he was on a sailing list. He told me this three months before I was ready to come home. He was down at the dock. This ship, they wouldn't let me on the ship. Naturally, he told me, you know what, brother, they're going to blow this island up. My right arm to God, he's been dead for a few years now, but that's what he told me. He said they're going to blow this island up. By God, he was right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why did he think that?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Little different things was adding up, adding up, adding up. Mostly maybe why he said that, yeah, but they called Clausen, down Ft. Kamehameha, secret, 12-inch disappearing guns they had imbedded on the ground. They'd recoil up out of the ground, shoot and shoot, go back in the ground. He was telling me about it. He said keep this to yourself. He said this is -- they're going to blow them ships out of the water when they try to come in here, but they're going to blow this island up. This is what he told me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This was two years before?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yep. Three months before and he's buried in Arlington National Cemetery he retired as a master -- sergeant major. He was an Army career man. When he left Hawaii three months before the war started. War started, they shipped him to Germany, Patton's 3rd Army. He ended up -- didn't go back to the Pacific. Patton's 3rd Army, that's where he ended up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So he ended up in Europe?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: In Europe, yep. Germany. Never got a scratch. Never got a scratch.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Had to go through the Bulge and the whole thing?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah, he went through the whole war. Never got a scratch.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Lucky.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: But he told me, I swear to God. I can still hear him telling me they're going to blow this island up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, let me make sure I heard that. That was three months before?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Three months before, yeah. Three months before. When I enlisted, I got to Scofield barracks. When I could -- I wasn't on duty, I phoned him down at Ft. Kamehameha. I said, "You know who this is?" He says, "No." I said, "Your brother, Jim." He called me Jimmy boy. I said, "Your brother, Jimmy boy." He says, "What? What the hell you doing down here?" I says, "Soldiering, just like you." He couldn't believe till he come up to the barracks to see me. He was already a sergeant. I was only a buck private then. I ended up out ranking him. He was -- he only had three up. I had three up and one down. I ended up as a staff sergeant. He couldn't believe it. He was a career. Ft. France, Wyoming; Ft. Myers, Virginia. He had been in the Army for years before I enlisted and I outranked him. He says you little -- I was bigger than him, but you know my brother. He says, "You little..." I said, "See 'em, Buddy? There's three up, one down." Actually, if I would have been his boss, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: He was only a buck sergeant then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about mail call, getting letters from home?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: That was the most wonderful thing in the world, any -- a letter from anybody. That was the most wonderful thing in the world.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any specific memories of mail, letters or packages?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Never got a package. Yes, I did. One time I got one carton of Lucky Strikes from my older sister. One carton of Lucky Strikes. One more thing about Hawaii. When the war started, I had the command car for my battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Reese. About six miles there was no road. You couldn't go clear around the island at Oahu at that time. There was about six miles, just railroad, narrow-gauge railroad. He said, "I'll tell you one thing, fellow. We're going to go around the island." We come down this railroad track. He said, "We can say we was the first son of a guns that went around the island." I'll tell you one more story. Guadalcanal, we had the Lungo river and I mean this command car, we come to this little opening like between the trees. He says, "Buddy, let's cross the river." I said, "What?" He said, "Let's cross the river. Let's see if we can get across the river." I said, "You mean with the command car?" He says, "Yeah." We had mud coming up over top the hood. We had to get a big army truck with a wench to wench us out. Somebody says, "Sergeant, you got no sense than to cross the river?" I said, "No, it was the major" -- or "lieutenant colonel didn't have better sense. He was the man told me to drive across the river. Somebody didn't have any sense. Water was clean over the hood --"

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Jim had a lot of things that went down with that boat or ship, so he didn't bring any things home with him.

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: I had a beautiful Army 45 from the Jap bomber. I had the plexiglas carved out for the handles. It had a naked girl on each side. Guys offered me --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: From a Jap bomber?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where did you get that?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: Guadalcanal. Guys offered me different things for it. No, it went down to the bottom of the ocean.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why was your stuff still on the ship if you weren't there?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: This was a ship. Transport didn't have room for everything. They had another cargo ship that they loaded all our personal stuff on the ship. Between the South Pacific and San Francisco somewhere -- it was an Army transport name of McCauley.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was torpedoed?

sp.speaker: James Workman
sp.p: They torpedoed it. You know, in Hawaii, they blamed Admiral Kimmel and General Short. They were the two commanders. They blamed them for not being prepared. They put out -- I'll never forget. They put out on our bulletin board. Don't be caught Short with your Kimmel. Don't be caught Short with your Kimmel. You know, life's crazy, you can remember things that happened 60 some years ago and you can't remember what you did yesterday. That's crazy.
